pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Habitats & Basic Needs

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants, and how they depend on each other.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-ESS3-1 / 2-LS4-1):** K-ESS3-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1] or [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-1]'; 2-LS4-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1].'

- **Operational details:** Building on 'what living things need' (food, water, air, shelter, suitable conditions), children connect each need to a feature of the habitat that supplies it (a pond gives a frog water, food and shelter), and take a first step into interdependence — organisms in a habitat rely on EACH OTHER (bees pollinate flowers; flowers feed bees). The key move is causal matching of need → habitat feature, and recognising that an organism placed where its needs aren't met cannot survive.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B (concrete, first causal/relational reasoning). Success = explaining WHY a specific habitat suits an organism by naming which need each feature meets, giving at least one 'depend on each other' example, and predicting failure when a habitat doesn't meet a need — not merely matching animal to place by appearance.
bestPractices: Anchor every match to a NEED–FEATURE link ('the pond gives the frog water AND insects to eat'), not just 'frogs live in ponds'.
Introduce interdependence concretely with a mutual pair (bee–flower, worm–soil) before any abstract 'web' language.
Use a mismatch/prediction move ('what happens if we put the fish on the sand?') so suitability is felt as consequence, not decoration.
Compare contrasting habitats (pond, desert, woodland) so 'suited to' means different needs met in different ways.
Start from local, observable habitats before exotic ones so the idea is grounded in first-hand experience.
keyRepresentations: A needs–checklist overlaid on a habitat scene (food ✓, water ✓, shelter ✓, conditions ✓).
Need→feature arrows linking an organism's needs to the parts of the habitat that supply them.
A mutual-dependence pair diagram (bee ↔ flower) showing each gives the other something.
Contrasting habitat cards (pond / desert / woodland) with the same needs met differently.
commonMisconceptions: Matching animal to habitat by appearance or familiarity, without linking to needs.
Thinking any animal could survive anywhere if it 'tried'.
Seeing organisms as independent — missing that they depend on each other, not just on the physical place.
Believing plants don't have needs or a habitat in the same sense as animals.
Treating 'habitat' as only the shelter/home rather than the whole life-supporting place.

learn.summary: For ages 6–8, teach that organisms live in habitats suited to them because each habitat feature supplies a specific basic need (food, water, shelter, suitable conditions), and that living things depend on each other, not only on the place. The central move is causal need→feature matching plus predicting failure when a need is unmet, rather than matching animal to place by appearance. Plants, like animals, have needs met by a habitat. Interdependence is introduced concretely with a mutual organism pair before any abstract 'web' language.

activities.title: Build-a-habitat: match every need to a feature
feedback: If a learner says 'frogs just live in ponds,' ask: 'Which need does the pond meet — and name more than one.' Push for water AND food AND shelter.
If a learner predicts the frog will 'get used to' the desert, return to what living things need: a place is only a habitat if it meets those needs; name which ones the desert fails.
If a learner thinks only animals have needs, use the pond-weed case to show a plant also fails in a habitat that lacks water or suitable conditions.
When a learner designs the new creature's home, check each of the four needs is explicitly tied to a feature; a gap means the home is not yet suitable.
Reinforce: naming WHICH need fails in a mismatch is the sign of real understanding, not just saying 'it won't work.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring every match to a need–feature link, comparing contrasting habitats, and using a mismatch/prediction move make suitability felt as consequence. Including a plant case counters the belief that only animals have needs. An interactive bench where need ticks turn green (met) or red (unmet) as a child places the organism can make the recompute concrete; this is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required medium — the same reasoning works with habitat cards and a spoken checklist.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2: 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants, and how they depend on each other.'

learnerActions: Place an organism (e.g. a frog) into different habitats — pond, desert, woodland — and for each one go through a four-item needs checklist: food, water, shelter, suitable conditions.
For each need, name the specific habitat feature that supplies it, or mark it unmet: e.g. 'the pond gives the frog water, insects to eat, and reeds to hide in.'

Also work a plant case: place pond weed and ask whether it could move to the desert — name which needs (water, suitable conditions) the desert fails, so plants are seen to have needs and a habitat just as animals do.
Predict out loud what happens when a need is unmet — e.g. a pond frog in a dry desert has no pond water and no damp place to keep its skin moist, so it cannot survive there.
Finally, design a suitable home for a new creature and defend it need-by-need, stating which feature meets each need.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Suited to' means every basic need is met by something in the habitat; an organism placed where a need cannot be met cannot survive. Suitability is a causal consequence, not decoration or appearance. Plants as well as animals have needs met by their habitat.

activities.title: Depend on each other: the mutual pair
feedback: If a learner lists pond organisms separately, prompt: 'How does the insect help the frog? How do the plants help the insect?' Build the chain link by link.
If a learner only says what an animal takes, ask what it gives back, so dependence is seen as mutual.
When the bees are removed, confirm the learner can trace the consequence all the way to a dependent animal's food, not just to the flowers.
If a learner treats soil like a living partner, clarify that worm–soil is an organism depending on its habitat, while bee–flower is two living things depending on each other.
activities.rationale: Introducing interdependence with a concrete mutual organism pair before abstract web language, and tracing one dependency chain, matches how first causal/relational reasoning develops at this tier. A live toggle that removes pollinators and flips a dependent animal's food tick is an optional way to make the chain visible; the chain can equally be traced on paper or in discussion.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2: 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants, and how they depend on each other.'
learnerActions: Study a mutual-dependence pair of living things — bee and flower — and state what each gives the other (bees pollinate flowers so they make seeds/fruit; flowers feed bees).
Trace one dependency chain in a pond — pond plants feed insects, insects feed the frog — and say which organism relies on which.

Explore 'remove the bees' as a thought-experiment: flowers that rely on bees to carry their pollen would make fewer seeds and fruit, so an animal that fed on those seeds or fruit could lose some of its food. Say which need flips to unmet and why. (Some plants, like grasses, are pollinated by the wind instead, and other animals besides bees can also pollinate.)
Name one thing the frog gives back to the pond, not just what it takes, to see dependence running both ways.

(Extension) Note that a worm also depends on its soil habitat — the soil gives it food and shelter and the worm enriches the soil — but recognise soil is part of the habitat, not another living partner like the bee and flower.
activities.intendedInsight: Living things depend on each other, not only on the physical place; removing one organism can take away another organism's met need. Interdependence between organisms is a concrete relationship before it is an abstract 'web.'

activities.title: Talk it through as the organism
feedback: If the proposed home 'sounds fine,' insist on naming the exact need that is missing — vague 'it won't like it' is not enough.
For the woodlouse case, check the learner names the lost damp conditions rather than just saying it would not like the path.
Prompt for a 'depend on each other' example in every explanation, not only the physical place.
activities.rationale: Speaking the needs reasoning and defending a proposed home builds production, not just recognition. The woodlouse case checks transfer to a new organism. A talking-animal persona can prompt needs reasoning but tends to present matches rather than let the learner test a mismatch, so pair it with hands-on placing/designing.
learnerActions: Take the role of an organism: 'I'm a frog — what do I need, and where in my habitat do I get each thing?'
Have a partner (or the learner) propose a different home for the creature, then say which specific need would fail there and why.
Transfer to a new case: a woodlouse lives under a damp log — say what would happen to it on a hot, dry path and which need (damp shelter/suitable conditions) fails.
Say aloud a full explanation: name each need, the feature that meets it, and at least one way the organism depends on another organism.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to say, in your own words, which need each feature meets and which need a wrong place fails shows the matching is understood, not memorised, and transfers to new organisms.

activities.title: Check and score: which need fails?
feedback: Correct response names specific missing needs (water, damp conditions and damp shelter, plus pond food such as insects if the field lacks them) and predicts the frog cannot survive — not merely 'no' or 'it will adapt.'
If the learner says the frog 'will get used to it,' reteach the prerequisite: what living things actually need, then match each need to what the field lacks.
If the learner treats habitat as only 'a home to sit in,' broaden it to the whole place-that-provides and list the several needs it meets.
activities.rationale: Matching with a follow-up asking which need fails probes need–feature reasoning rather than appearance-based pairing. Recognition-style sorting and multiple-choice items can assess and score classification but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an explanation, so use alongside the design and talk-through tasks.
learnerActions: Match organisms to habitats, then answer a follow-up that asks WHICH need fails in a wrong pairing — e.g. 'Why can't a cactus live in a pond?' or 'Why can't a fish live on the sand?'
Sort features of a habitat by which need they meet (food, water, shelter, conditions).
Answer: 'A frog lives in a pond. It is moved to a dry, sunny field with no water. Will it be okay — and what exactly did the pond give that the field does not?'
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer names the specific needs the new place fails to provide; treating places as interchangeable or naming no need signals a misconception.

constraints: Start from local, observable habitats before exotic ones so the idea is grounded in first-hand experience.
Always anchor a match to a need–feature link, never 'animal X lives in place Y' by appearance or familiarity.
Introduce interdependence with a concrete mutual organism pair first (bee–flower); delay abstract 'food web' language.

Recognition tasks (matching, sorting, multiple-choice) can assess and reinforce classification but do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation; include a design/explain task for production.
A tap-to-reveal habitat presents matches as pre-decided; it is a useful pre-teach or reference but does not itself let the learner test suitability or feel a mismatch.

Interactive ticks, toggles, and animated consequences are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — habitat cards, paper checklists, and spoken reasoning carry the same logic and should not be treated as inferior.
Include plants as having needs and a habitat in the same sense as animals, and work at least one plant case with learners, to counter the belief that only animals do.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D exploration as adding 'cost without deepening the insight' and implied 2D is simply better. Softened: the learning is relational, so a walk-through is only worthwhile if it genuinely helps a child spot need-meeting features — a scoped trade-off, not a universal claim that 3D adds nothing.

The original framed the interactive 'recompute' as uniquely able to make suitability 'felt rather than stated.' Retained as an optional concrete mechanism; the underlying reasoning is medium-independent and achievable with cards and discussion.

The assessment correct answer notes the pond gives the frog water 'to breathe/live in'; frogs breathe air via lungs and absorb oxygen through moist skin rather than breathing water like fish. For this age, emphasise water to keep skin moist and as the place it lives; the imprecise 'breathe the water' wording is not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

The original offered 'worm–soil' as a mutual-dependence pair; soil is part of the habitat, not another living organism, so it is reframed as an organism depending on its habitat, with bee–flower kept as the organism-to-organism example of 'depend on each other.'

The NGSS K-ESS3-1 source is marked verified:false in the row; its citation is retained only as unconfirmed and should not be treated as established support, while the verified DfE claim is the primary support.

probeDeeper: The pond has frogs, insects and pond weed. How do they depend on each other?
Could you move the pond weed to the desert instead? Why not?
A woodlouse lives under a damp log. What would happen to it on a hot, dry path? Why?
Name one thing the frog gives back to the pond, not just what it takes.
assess.correctAnswer: The frog will not be okay. A habitat provides everything an organism needs: the pond gave water (to keep its skin moist and to breathe/live in), food such as insects, and shelter. The dry field meets none of these, so the frog cannot survive. A good answer names specific needs the new place fails to provide.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It'll be fine, it'll just get used to it' — believes an animal can live anywhere and adapts to any place within its lifetime; places seen as interchangeable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to what living things actually need to survive (the prerequisite), then match each need to what the pond supplies and the field lacks; a place is only a habitat if it meets the needs.
errorPatterns.distractor: The frog will be fine — it will just get used to living in the field.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the frog survives the field, with no need named, or says it will 'learn to live there'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A habitat is just the animal's home/house' — thinks a habitat is only the den or spot the animal sits in, not the surrounding place that supplies food, water and other organisms.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden 'habitat' from a single home to the whole place-that-provides; list the several needs the pond meets, not just shelter.
errorPatterns.distractor: The pond just gives the frog a home to sit in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked what the pond gives, says 'somewhere to live/sit' but cannot name food, water, or other organisms it depends on.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Each animal lives on its own' — does not see interdependence; treats the frog, insects and pond plants as unconnected.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one dependency chain in the pond (plants→insects→frog) and one mutual pair; make 'depend on each other' concrete before naming it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the interdependence probe, lists pond organisms separately and cannot say how they rely on each other.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks organisms can live anywhere or that a habitat is just a home; cannot connect the place to the organism's needs.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the pond meets several specific needs AND describes at least one interdependence (frog eats insects, insects live on pond plants), then transfers the needs-place logic to a new organism such as the woodlouse.
responseLevels.partial: Says the frog needs the pond and names one need (usually water), but lists needs in isolation and does not describe how the pond's organisms depend on each other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the child: 'A frog lives in a pond. I scoop it up and move it to a dry, sunny field where there is no water.' Ask: 'Will the frog be okay there? Why or why not — and what exactly did the pond give the frog that the field does not?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks animals simply 'get used to' wherever they are says the frog will be fine — they treat places as interchangeable. A child who understands a habitat as the provider of specific needs predicts the frog fails AND names which needs (water, food, damp shelter) are missing. Naming the needs is only possible with the correct model.
